html:
The Battle of Cerignola was fought on 28 April 1503 outside the town of Cerignola in Apulia, southern Italy. A Spanish army under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, called the Great Captain, beat a French army. It is often called the first battle in Europe won by handheld guns.

France and Spain had agreed to divide the Kingdom of Naples and then fought over the shares, as part of the Italian Wars. Córdoba took a position on a slope among vineyards. His men dug a ditch along the front and piled the earth into a bank. Behind it he placed about 1,000 arquebusiers, backed by German pikemen. The French, with heavy armoured cavalry and Swiss pikemen, arrived late in the day and attacked at once. The horsemen could not cross the ditch and were shot down at close range. Their commander, the Duke of Nemours, was among the first killed. The battle lasted about an hour.

Spain took Naples and kept it for two centuries. Cerignola showed that foot soldiers with guns, behind earthworks, could stop both knights and pikes. Córdoba's mixed units of pike and shot grew into the Spanish tercios, which dominated European battlefields until Rocroi.
